statement: Traffic congestion is becoming a serious problem in many towns and cities around the world.
question: What problems does this cause? What solutions can you suggest?
model:
In cities from Jakarta to Los Angeles, motorists may spend the equivalent of several working days each year sitting in stationary traffic. Congestion damages health, the economy and quality of life, yet experience shows that it can be eased through well-designed transport policies.

The effects of gridlock are wide-ranging. Most directly, it wastes time: commuters who spend two hours a day in traffic have less time for their families, exercise and rest, which contributes to stress and fatigue. Businesses suffer too, since delayed deliveries and unreliable journey times add to costs that are eventually passed on to consumers. Perhaps most seriously, vehicles idling in queues release large quantities of exhaust fumes, and air pollution in congested cities is linked to asthma, heart disease and thousands of premature deaths. Emergency services can also be dangerously delayed when ambulances cannot get through.

The most effective long-term solution is to offer people attractive alternatives to the car. Frequent, affordable and reliable public transport, such as the metro systems of Seoul or Madrid, can carry far more passengers than roads ever could. Safe, separated cycle lanes have transformed travel in Copenhagen, where more residents now commute by bicycle than by car. Urban planning matters as well: when homes, shops and workplaces are built close together, many journeys can be made on foot.

Alongside these improvements, governments may need to discourage unnecessary driving. Congestion charges, like those introduced in London and Stockholm, reduce traffic in city centres and raise money that can be reinvested in public transport. Encouraging flexible working hours would also spread journeys more evenly through the day.

In conclusion, traffic congestion harms people's health, wastes their time and slows economic activity. By investing in public transport and cycling while making driving into city centres less attractive, authorities can make urban areas cleaner and far easier to move around.
